arguments.heading: Argument analysis for the March 25, 2026 session
paragraphs: Flowers asked the Court to adopt a bright-line approach tied to cross-border transportation and vehicle interaction. They said Brock’s last-leg, intrastate work falls outside the Section 1 exemption.
Brock asked the Court to reject any vehicle-interaction requirement and to recognize last-leg drivers as covered by the exemption. Both sides agreed to confine this case to the bright-line issue.

Flowers reasoned that transportation is bounded by loading and unloading on a cross-border vehicle, and that unloading marks the end. In a drivers example, they said only the second driver would be exempt.
Brock reasoned that the journey is continuous until goods reach retail stores, even on an intrastate leg. He relied on Supreme Court cases to ground the meaning of engaged in commerce.

The justices tested assumptions about the shipment’s final destination and worker categorization. They asked where the bread ends its trip and about splitting interstate shipments into different worker categories.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: The dispute asks whether to adopt a clear rule for who counts as working in interstate commerce, based on crossing borders or interacting with vehicles that cross.
The argument centered on last-leg delivery of bread to stores. A justice asked where the bread’s journey ends. The answer said the retail stores are the final stop.

sections.heading: How the case got here
paragraphs: The Supreme Court heard the case on March 25, 2026. Traci L. Lovitt argued for Flowers Foods. Jennifer D. Bennett argued for Angelo Brock.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: Flowers asks the Court to limit the Section 1 exemption to workers who directly and actively do cross-border transportation. They say Brock only performs intrastate last-leg work, so he is not exempt.

Flowers also asks for a bright-line rule that requires either crossing a border or interacting with vehicles that do. They focus on the class’s cross-border transportation work. They assume last-mile framing here.
Brock asks the Court to hold that the exemption covers drivers who move goods on the last leg of an interstate journey. He says border crossing and vehicle interaction do not matter and are atextual.
Brock agrees that this case should resolve only the bright-line rule question that both sides presented.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: Flowers frames transportation as bookended by loading and unloading on a cross-border vehicle. They say interacting with a cross-border vehicle often matters, even if no one crosses a border.
Flowers answered a drivers example by saying only the second driver would be exempt, because transportation continues until unloading at the end of the trip.
Brock says last-leg drivers are part of one continuous interstate journey that ends at retail stores. He accepts calling it the intrastate leg of an interstate journey.
Brock says Supreme Court cases support this meaning of engaged in commerce, and that those cases reflect how the phrase was understood at the time.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: The justices pressed both sides on the shipment’s endpoint and worker categories. They asked where the bread’s journey ends and what the final destination is in this case.

They raised concern about splitting workers on one interstate shipment into different categories. Flowers said only one driver in a multi-driver chain would be exempt. Brock said retail stores are the endpoint.
